chapter_theme: Intelligence-gathering is treated as the sight of the state and as a discipline of evidence: a spy must watch everyone and hold firm, and the king must not trust any one spy.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: its excellence (581), the duty it serves (582), the fault of neglecting it (583), the spy's characteristics (584-587), and how to employ spies, verify their reports, and reward them (588-590).

581.reading: Let a ruler hold spies and the well-regarded treatise, these two, firmly as his eyes.
581.nuance: Immediately after a chapter that defines the eye by kindness, the eye is redefined by information. Parimelazhagar's pairing makes the spy the eye of flesh, which sees what is happening, and the treatise the eye of wisdom, which says what to do about it.

582.reading: To know quickly, at all times, everything happening to everyone is the king's work.
582.nuance: Knowing is called the work itself. Parimelazhagar explains that this is a figure, since both favour and punishment depend on timely knowledge.

positions.position: 'Everyone' is the three classes named in 584, and what is known is their good and bad words and acts.
'Everyone' is the surrounding kings, whether enemy, ally, middle or neutral, and both their circle and his own.
positions.quote: பகைவராகியும் நட்டாராகியும் மத்திமராகியும் உதாசீனராகியும் இருக்கின்ற அரசர்க்கும்

583.reading: A ruler who does not gather through spies and discern what it all means has no victory lying ready to take.
583.nuance: The verse has two conditions: spying and discerning (பொருள் தெரியா). Gathering reports without weighing them fails as well.

584.reading: A spy is one who examines everyone: those doing the king's work, his kin, and those who wish him ill.
584.nuance: The list begins with the king's own servants and relatives; enemies come last. Surveillance turns inward first, and Kalaignar draws out of this a professional ethic: the spy must not sort people by favour.

585.reading: A spy is one who can take an appearance that raises no suspicion, not flinch before eyes that probe him, and never let anything spill.
585.nuance: உகாஅமை is the image of not spilling. Parimelazhagar's gloss shows his own social world: the unsuspected forms are those of Brahmins, merchants and the like.

586.reading: A spy goes in the guise of renunciants, pushes through to examine what must be examined, and gives nothing away whatever is done to him.
586.nuance: என்செயினும் quietly admits torture. Parimelazhagar sees this: having mentioned the four methods already, he says force is raised again because it is the hardest to bear.

positions.position: He lives as complete renunciants and vow-keepers such as pilgrims do, and this commentator records separately that others read படிவம் as costume.
positions.quote: இதனுள் 'படிவம்' என்றதனை வேடமாக்கி, 'துறந்தார் வேடத்தாராகி' என்று உரைப்பாரும் உளர்.

positions.position: He wears the costume of an ascetic and crosses the country's border to gather news.
positions.quote: தவஞ் செய்வார் வேடத்தராகி, நாட்டெல்லையைக் கடந்து போய்

positions.position: No renunciant is involved: he simply seems unconnected with the affair.

587.reading: A spy is one able to hear what has been concealed and to be free of doubt about what he has learned.
587.nuance: Parimelazhagar's reason is practical: a king can't act on a report delivered with doubt. The next verse then refuses to accept the spy's certainty, so in this chapter confidence is required of the source but not trusted by the user.

588.reading: Even what a spy has found and brought back should be confirmed through another spy.
588.nuance: The commentators explain why from a suspicion of corruption: Parimelazhagar thinks of collusion with those being watched, and Manakkudavar of a spy taking money from rival kings.

589.reading: Run spies so that one does not know of another, and accept what three say in agreement.
589.nuance: This is a statement about independent evidence: agreement counts only among witnesses who could not have conferred. Parimelazhagar adds that agreement need only be in substance (பயனால்), and that if the accounts differ, the inquiry continues.

590.reading: Do not honour a spy where others can see it; if the king does, he has himself let out the secret.
590.nuance: The exposure comes from the patron, not the spy, and from gratitude, not carelessness: the honour itself is the leak. The verse does not forbid the reward, only its being seen.

links.note: Both name two things as a person's eyes. 392 gives every living person numbers and letters. 581 gives a ruler spies and the treatise. Each makes sight depend on something outside the body.

In adjacent chapters a ruler's eye is first the grace that spares and then the instrument that watches everyone, kin included (584). The Kural does not reconcile the two eyes, and 578 is the nearest it comes to a rule between them.

274 condemns hiding behind ascetic practice as a hunter hides in a bush to trap birds. 586 prescribes exactly that kind of cover for the state's spy, on Manakkudavar's reading at least. The Virtue book's hypocrisy becomes the Wealth book's technique.
423 tells the individual to find the truth whoever is speaking. 589 turns the same refusal to trust a source into a state procedure, with independence and counting as its method.

source_issues: 585: Manakkudavar's commentary is marked as not aligned in the source.
